abstract: Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries Dashboard, the monthly-updated public dashboard built on anonymized ADP payroll data covering 4.6 million workers across more than 730 occupations, released its July 2026 update on July 22, 2026 (data through June 2026, vintage 2026-07-16). Headline reading: across all ages, every exposure quintile now shows employment growth since ChatGPT (Nov 2022), but the pace is slowest for the two most-exposed quintiles — +1.1%/yr annualized for the most-exposed vs +2.0%/yr for the least-exposed; on a year-over-year basis the most-exposed quintile is at -0.2%. The early-career divergence persists but has eased slightly: workers ages 22-25 in the most-exposed occupation quintile are contracting at an annualized 3.5%/yr since ChatGPT (vs 3.8%/yr in the April 2026 reading), and -4.3% over the past year. New in this release: a gender decomposition. Early-career women disproportionately work in AI-exposed occupations (43.8% in the most-exposed category vs 32.4% of men), and within the most-exposed quintile early-career women are contracting at 4.5%/yr vs 2.5%/yr for men. The lab attributes most of the gender gap to occupational composition rather than disparate within-occupation trends.
keyFindings: June 2026 data: all-ages employment growing in every exposure quintile since ChatGPT; most-exposed +1.1%/yr annualized vs +2.0%/yr least-exposed; most-exposed -0.2% YoY
Early-career (22-25) most-exposed quintile: -3.5%/yr annualized since ChatGPT (eased from -3.8%/yr in April 2026 reading); -4.3% over the past year
New gender analysis (updated July 22, 2026): early-career women in most-exposed quintile contracting 4.5%/yr vs 2.5%/yr for men since ChatGPT; past year -5.4% women vs -3.1% men
Composition: 43.8% of early-career women work in the most-exposed occupation category vs 32.4% of men — gender gap driven primarily by occupational mix, not within-occupation divergence
Occupation detail: early-career software developers and customer service reps show substantial declines; home health aides show early-career gains
Automation ratio (Anthropic Economic Index) correlates with employment declines; augmentation ratio shows no clear relationship
Methodology caveat from Feb 2026 update: with broadest controls, the decline in AI-exposed occupations only becomes significant in 2024; dashboard measures correlation, not causation
methodology: Monthly aggregation of anonymized ADP payroll records from a five-year balanced sample of firms (mitigating firm entry/exit), partitioned into quintiles by occupation-level AI exposure scores. Employment indexed to November 2022 (ChatGPT release). Published downloadable results include employment index, annualized growth since Nov 2022, and year-over-year change, by exposure quintile, age group, gender, and Anthropic Economic Index automation/augmentation ratios. Occupations matched via BLS 2018 SOC crosswalk.
qualifiers: Tier 1 — institutional-quality data infrastructure from Stanford DEL and ADP Research, drawing on the largest US payroll provider. ADP sample skews to medium and large private-sector employers; not nationally representative; balanced-firm design excludes firm entry/exit margins. The lab explicitly frames results as correlations between exposure measures and employment trends, not causal AI effects. Annualized and YoY figures are the lab's published CSV outputs (vintage 2026-07-16), not jobsdata.ai computations.
